spatial_claims.claim: A circle has rational diameter d; an equilateral pentagon, regular hexagon, and regular decagon are all inscribed in the same circle; the hexagon side equals the radius r = d/2.
The hexagon side r and decagon side s_10 satisfy the extreme-and-mean-ratio: (r + s_10) : r = r : s_10, yielding s_10^2 = r(r - s_10).
sq(s) = sq(r) + sq(s_10), i.e., the square on the pentagon side equals the sum of the squares on the hexagon and decagon sides (by 13.10).

configuration_map: Circle with rational diameter d and radius r = d/2. Three regular polygons inscribed in the same circle: pentagon (side s), hexagon (side s_6 = r), decagon (side s_10). No auxiliary geometric points are constructed in the plane. All subsequent quantities (N = s_10 + r/2, w = 2r - s_10 = 5r/2 - N) are algebraic expressions of lengths, not geometric constructions placed in the figure. The proof proceeds entirely through algebraic manipulation and Book 10 irrational-line classification after establishing the initial length relationships.
pass_reason: The proof makes only minimal spatial claims (three standard regular polygons inscribed in the same circle) which are mutually consistent. The bulk of the argument is algebraic: expressing the square on the pentagon side as a rectangle on a rational line, then classifying the breadth as a fourth apotome via Book 10 machinery. No angle decompositions, interior/exterior point claims, ray orderings, or betweenness claims are made. All cited geometric results (4.15, 13.1, 13.6, 13.9, 13.10) are standard and correctly applied. No spatial configuration contradiction exists.
